title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: New federal oversight push meets 55% Michigan opposition to nearby centers.

lines.text: Good morning and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.

It's Wednesday morning, August 5, and our big story today centers on U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten introducing federal legislation to require data center operators to report water and energy use while updating efficiency standards.
That comes right after a Sunday poll showed 55 percent of Michigan primary voters oppose data centers near their homes, with even higher numbers among Democrats.
Exactly, so let's unpack what this federal move means against the backdrop of local resistance we're seeing play out across the state right now.
Graham, walk me through the bills themselves. What exactly would they do?

Scholten's legislation would mandate annual surveys of how much power and water data centers actually consume, and it would push the Defense Department to tighten cooling requirements to safeguard water supplies, especially relevant here in Michigan with multiple projects under discussion.
Why introduce this now? Is it tied to the growing number of local fights we've covered?

It lines up with the timing. The poll from Sunday showed clear voter concern over electric bills and water use, and we've seen concrete actions like Augusta Township residents voting today to kill a farmland rezoning for a data center.
That vote in Augusta keeps the land agricultural and avoids the noise, power, and water demands. How does a federal reporting requirement change the game for places like that?

It adds transparency at the national level, so operators can't keep impacts hidden. Local voters already used their voices in Augusta to block the shift to industrial use, and similar scrutiny is happening elsewhere.
Independence Township also acted today with a moratorium on new proposals while they write rules. That gives Oakland County residents time to figure out limits on power, water, and land use.

Right, and that moratorium creates a template other townships might follow. The federal bills could complement that by forcing data on resource use that communities can then use in their own planning.
What about the history here? How long have these local battles been building?

They've been escalating this week and last. Yesterday Lowell City Council ended talks with Microsoft over secrecy on power needs, and the city halted utilities negotiations with the township, leaving the project without water supply.
That uncertainty in Kent County hits jobs, taxes, and grid strain all at once. And we had the Wayne County $6 billion proposal surface yesterday too.

Yes, that one would bring construction jobs but heavy electricity demand. Officials there haven't scheduled a formal review yet, so residents are watching for tax revenue versus potential rate impacts.
Meanwhile, yesterday's report on the governor facing scrutiny over a Saline Township project advancing without all local approvals. How does that fit the bigger picture of local control?
It puts the spotlight on whether state-level support can move forward without township sign-off, and it comes as primary voters head to the polls with those resource concerns top of mind.
The poll numbers are striking — 63 percent opposition among likely Democratic primary voters. What does that tell us about where the pressure is coming from?

It shows broad skepticism on who pays higher electric bills and handles water use. DTE Energy noted yesterday that landing large data-center loads is key to holding down rates long-term, so the stakes for households are real either way.
And the Washtenaw recalls filed Monday against seven officials over these same issues. Voters 30 miles away will be watching if those reach the ballot.
That recall effort stems directly from fights over power, water, and taxes. It shows how these projects are mobilizing residents at the hyper-local level.
So the federal bills could give communities more data to push back or negotiate. But what happens next with Scholten's legislation?
It would go through Congress, likely facing debates on federal versus state roles. In the meantime, more townships are pausing like Independence did today, buying time to set their own standards.
And the farmland protection angle in Augusta today really highlights the land-use tension. How many other agricultural areas might see similar votes?
It's a pattern we're tracking statewide. The poll suggests residents 30 to 60 miles from any project are paying attention because grid strain and water demands don't stay hyper-local.
If the bills pass, annual reporting could reveal whether these centers are efficient enough to justify the infrastructure asks. What are the odds it moves quickly?
Hard to say, but the timing with the poll and these local wins like Augusta gives it momentum. Lawmakers will be watching how communities respond in the coming weeks.
Shifting to quick hits, Graham, let's start with today's Augusta Township vote. Residents overturned that rezoning and blocked the project outright.
Yes, and it directly spares Washtenaw County taxpayers and homeowners the noise, power, and water demands that would have followed.
Also today, Independence Township approved a moratorium stopping new proposals while rules get written. That's a pause for Oakland County residents to decide limits.
It gives them breathing room on how much power, water, and land these projects can use going forward.
Yesterday in Lowell, the city council stopped all Microsoft talks citing secrecy on power needs and local impacts.
That blocks one of the few large-scale projects discussed in West Michigan this year, leaving Kent County residents with uncertainty on jobs and grid strain.
Same day, Lowell city officials suspended sewer and water negotiations with the township, halting progress on that data center.
It signals growing resistance to projects that could strain resources and raise utility rates for residents.
Also yesterday, a new report questions whether Gov. Whitmer advanced the Saline Township project before all local permits were secured.
Residents in Washtenaw County could see big changes in power demand, water use, and tax revenue if it moves ahead.
And the Wayne County $6 billion proposal landed on the table yesterday, promising thousands of construction jobs but heavy electricity demand.
Local officials haven't scheduled a formal review yet, so the balance of tax gains versus grid strain is still up in the air.
Monday's DTE filing tied future rate stability to landing those large data-center loads.
Their pipeline stayed steady even as demand forecasts rise, meaning Michigan households could feel it in bills depending on whether campuses come online or stall.
And the Washtenaw recall bids filed Monday against seven officials over these projects.
The effort comes from fights on power, water, and taxes, and voters elsewhere will watch if they reach the ballot.
Now for on deck, Graham, any public meetings coming up that listeners should know about?
No major data center hearings are listed on the tracker for today or tomorrow, but township boards often add items quickly.
Residents should check their local calendars or the Michigan Data Center Tracker for any last-minute agendas on rezonings or moratorium extensions.
That's the practical next step while these federal bills and local votes play out.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Scholten's Federal Bills on Data Center Reporting Amid Voter Pushback
